# testdata

## `supplemental/` — the independent known-answer corpus

### Provenance

`supplemental/` is not this fork's work. It is a copy of
`fastfloat/supplemental_test_files` at commit
`088643e8d5010bd3d1540fe48685601b43b9a3e5`, vendored into this tree. That is the
repository fast_float's own test suite reads: upstream `tests/basictest.cpp`
carries `TEST_CASE("supplemental")` at `:557`, which iterates
`SUPPLEMENTAL_TEST_DATA_DIR` and calls `check_file` on every entry, and this
fork's `tests.zig` consumes the same files.

### Credit and licence

The corpus states its own credit and its own licence, in its own README, in five
lines that are carried here verbatim. Read out of the vendored
`supplemental/README.md`:

1. The title line: `# supplemental_test_files`.
2. `Supplemental data files for testing floating parsing (credit: Nigel Tao for
   the data)` — the data is **Nigel Tao's**, and the donor says so itself.
3. A blank line.
4. `LICENSE file (Apache 2):` — the grant is **Apache-2.0**, and it is the only
   one; there is no alternative to choose between, unlike upstream's triple.
5. The URL that follows it,
   <https://github.com/nigeltao/parse-number-fxx-test-data/blob/main/LICENSE>,
   which is the producer's own copy of that licence.

`fastfloat/supplemental_test_files` is a hosting location, not the identity of
the work, so the credit goes to the producer and not to the host repository.

### What was vendored, and where the licence text came from

The donor repository at that commit holds **fifteen** files: the thirteen data
files, its `README.md` and its `CMakeLists.txt`. It has **no `LICENSE` file of
its own**, so `supplemental/LICENSE` is not a donor byte and calling it one
would be false.

`supplemental/LICENSE` is the Apache License 2.0 text this fork took from the
producer's own copy at the URL the donor README names. It is unedited, and it is
byte-distinct from this repository's `LICENSE-APACHE` (11,323 bytes against
10,767): the fork's copy carries upstream's `Copyright 2021 The fast_float
authors` line at `:178` and the corpus copy does not, so neither file can stand
in for the other.

That makes sixteen files in the directory: fifteen donor files vendored byte for
byte, plus one separately sourced licence text. All sixteen are hashed in
`UPSTREAM.sha256`, so the licence text cannot be dropped without the record
failing. `NOTICE.md` § "The known-answer corpus is a separate Apache-2.0 work"
carries the same statement for a reader who does not come here.

### What the fork reads, and what it does not

`data/` holds thirteen files, 5,268,191 lines, 274,299,340 bytes. All thirteen
are present and all thirteen are readable; the file names carry the producing
project, not a guarantee about this fork.

`tests.zig` reads **nine** of the thirteen, in full, every line:

| file | lines | producer of the expected bits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `google-double-conversion.txt` | 564,745 | Google's `double-conversion` |
| `ulfjack-ryu.txt` | 599,458 | Ryū's shortest round-trip printing |
| `ibm-fpgen.txt` | 102,792 | IBM's hex-float parser test generator |
| `lemire-fast-double-parser.txt` | 94,313 | Daniel Lemire's `fast_double_parser` |
| `google-wuffs.txt` | 10,744 | Wuffs |
| `freetype-2-7.txt` | 3,566 | FreeType 2.7 |
| `lemire-fast-float.txt` | 3,299 | Daniel Lemire's `fast_float` |
| `tencent-rapidjson.txt` | 3,563 | Tencent RapidJSON |
| `more-test-cases.txt` | 3 | hand-written |

That is 1,382,483 lines, and it is the set `tests.zig` iterates — at both widths,
on every line, in both the Debug and the ReleaseSafe run. The four
`remyoudompheng-fptest-{0,1,2,3}.txt` files are **not** read: 3,885,708 lines,
197,668,870 bytes, all generated by one producer (Remy Oudompheng's fptest
generator) rather than four. Their bit patterns are covered by the eight
independent producers above at a fraction of the read cost. The exclusion is a
cost decision recorded here so a reader does not mistake absence for oversight.

**Carrying a file this fork does not read leaves its licence question open, so
it is answered here rather than assumed.** The four files are inside the corpus
directory the grant above covers: the vendored `supplemental/README.md` credits
Nigel Tao for "the data" without naming files, and these four are part of that
data, vendored here from the same donor commit as the other thirteen and
hashed with them in `UPSTREAM.sha256`. They are therefore under the same
Apache-2.0 grant as the nine read files and as the licence text beside them —
read and unread are the same legal question here, and no separate permission
for Rémy Oudompheng's generator is claimed or needed, because the fork
redistributes the generated files and the grant is on those.

### Format, as read before anything was written against it

Every line in all thirteen files is

```
HHHH HHHHHHHH HHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH <decimal string>\n
```

four lowercase-or-uppercase hex digits, a space, eight hex digits, a space,
sixteen hex digits, a space, then the decimal string to the end of the line.
That is 31 bytes of fixed columns before the number. Measured over all
5,268,191 lines: zero lines deviate from
`^[0-9A-Fa-f]{4} [0-9A-Fa-f]{8} [0-9A-Fa-f]{16} [^ ]`, zero lines contain `CR`,
and every file ends with `LF`.

The three hex columns are the binary16, binary32 and binary64 IEEE 754 bit
patterns of the decimal string, most significant byte first, so a reader that
wants a `u32` or a `u64` from a column has to read the bytes big-endian. This is
upstream's own layout, not an inference: `tests/basictest.cpp:444-455` parses
the 32-bit column with `std::from_chars(str.data() + 5, ..., float32, 16)`, the
64-bit column from `str.data() + 14`, and takes the decimal string from
`str.data() + 31`. `tests.zig` uses the same offsets.

The binary16 column is not used by this fork. `parse_number.h` has no half
precision path for these types, and upstream's own reader only reads that column
under `#ifdef __STDCPP_FLOAT16_T__` (`tests/basictest.cpp:434-443`).

### Range outcomes recorded in the corpus

A line whose number overflows or underflows records the bit pattern the parse
is expected to *end up with*, not the bit pattern of the number written. Both
appear in the corpus: `1e681` is recorded as `7F800000 7FF0000000000000`
(infinity at both widths) and `0.2e-5678` as `00000000 0000000000000000`
(zero at both widths). So a conforming parser must store the rounded value and
*additionally* report the range condition; upstream does exactly that, storing
via `to_float` at `parse_number.h:288` before setting
`std::errc::result_out_of_range` at `:292`. `tests.zig` therefore accepts either
the typed surface's success or its `ResultOutOfRange` for such a line, and checks
the bits in both cases, which is the same rule upstream's own `check_file`
applies (`tests/basictest.cpp:474-482`). For the out-of-range lines the value can
only be read through the raw C surface, because the typed surface reports the
condition and withholds a value the caller did not write; that is why
`tests.zig` uses `fast_float.c` there and nowhere else in the corpus loop.

### Independent cross-check of the corpus, and what it found

A recorded bit pattern is only an independent answer if it is the correctly
rounded value, so the whole corpus was checked before any of it was used as an
oracle. Each decimal string was converted two ways and both results were
compared with the recorded column, over all 5,268,191 lines of all thirteen
files: once through NumPy's `float64` and `float32` string parsing, and once
through an exact rational conversion with round-half-to-even carried out on
`Fraction`.

* **binary64 column: agrees with both conversions on all 5,268,191 lines.**
* **binary32 column: agrees on 5,268,175 lines. Sixteen lines disagree — and
  every one of the sixteen is a disagreement between NumPy's binary32
  conversion and the exact rational conversion, not between either of them and
  the corpus.** In all sixteen the exact rational conversion is the one that
  agrees with the recorded column. Each is an input whose binary32 result sits
  within half an ulp of a tie, which is where a conversion path that computes in
  wider precision first can land on the other side of the midpoint.

The sixteen, by file and 1-based line number, with both opinions. The numbers are
the ones a file viewer shows, so every row below can be checked against the
vendored bytes directly — the decimal in the third column and the pattern in the
fourth are both on the line named in the second column.

| file | line | decimal | recorded | NumPy binary32 | exact round-half-to-even |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `google-double-conversion.txt` | 236646 | `2.1665680640000002384185791015625e9` | `4f012335` | `4f012334` | `4f012335` |

So both columns are used as an oracle on every line of every file this fork
reads, with no line excluded for being awkward. `tests.zig` also records the line
count of each file it reads and fails if the count differs, so a fixture that was
truncated, extended or reordered cannot pass quietly.

### What the cross-check is, and what the test run adds

The cross-check above is independent of this fork: every number in it was read
out of the files or computed by the NumPy and exact-rational conversions
described, and none of it came from running the fork. It is what makes the
corpus usable as an oracle at all.

The test run is a separate fact, and it is not a substitute. `tests.zig` reading
all 1,382,483 lines of the nine files at both widths and reporting each file's
line count, in Debug and again in ReleaseSafe, all 13 tests passing in both
(`local://foundation-expansion-fast_float-final-debug-97.log`,
`…-final-releasesafe-100.log`), is evidence that the vendored bytes are the
bytes this fork reads and that fast_float agrees with them. It is not how the
expected patterns were obtained, and it does not check the four unread files
beyond their digests.
